rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify poorly resolved pairs while minimizing early co-elution. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.
Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the unresolved pair responds to reduced steepness. This modest change should improve separation while keeping the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

The critical pair improved with a shallower gradient, so narrow the solvent window to reduce steepness further. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the added retention and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Narrow the gradient window another step to lift the critical pair above R = 1.5. The higher starting organic fraction should preserve a last-peak time below 10 minutes, while the first peak should remain adequately retained.
Injection 4 achieved the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Increase temperature by 5 C to seek a shorter fully resolved separation while testing the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity.

Return to the temperature that achieved full resolution, and raise phi0 one step to shorten retention. The slightly shallower gradient may preserve the critical pair’s resolution; the early pair has enough separation to test this stronger starting solvent.

Test whether a larger temperature increase carries the critical pair through an elution-order reversal and restores resolution while shortening the run. This also checks for new close pairs elsewhere; injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback.
At 60 C the original critical region separates, but a different pair nearly co-elutes. Test 55 C as a selectivity compromise that may resolve both regions while retaining the shorter analysis time.
Slightly reduce gradient steepness at 55 C to try to raise the remaining R = 1.41 pair above 1.5. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves room for a modest retention increase without a time penalty.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek a shorter fully resolved run than injection 9. The narrower window also reduces gradient steepness, but the early pair and both temperature-sensitive middle pairs need checking.

Lowering phi0 should improve the early separation and may help the middle pair that deteriorated at phi0 = 0.20. Combine this with a steeper gradient to seek a substantially shorter run, while checking whether both critical middle pairs remain resolved.

Reduce steepness relative to injection 11 to improve the R = 1.29 pair while retaining a substantial time advantage over injection 9. Check that the other close middle pair, currently at R = 1.61, remains fully resolved.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction restores the critical separation seen in injection 11 while retaining its steeper, faster gradient. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed method with maximum CRF.

Explore a lower-temperature selectivity regime with a faster gradient to seek another route to a shorter fully resolved separation. Injection 13 already achieves maximum CRF and remains the fastest confirmed benchmark.

Test a substantially steeper gradient at 60 C to see whether the close middle pair separates on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover. This explores a much faster method while retaining injection 13 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF fallback.

Test an intermediate cooler temperature with a fast gradient: 25 C produced several co-elutions, while 40 C favored separation elsewhere but left one critical pair. At 35 C, temperature-dependent selectivity may balance those competing pairs and yield full resolution in roughly seven minutes.

Explore a fast gradient at the untested 50 C setting to look for favorable selectivity after the middle-pair order reversal. The lower starting organic fraction protects early retention; injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test the grid midpoint between injections 11 and 12, where the limiting pair improved from R = 1.29 to 1.67. This should approach full resolution with a last-peak time near 7.6 minutes, providing a faster alternative to injection 12.

Shorten the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method by two gradient minutes to test its speed limit directly. This isolates the effect of steepness on its two near-threshold middle pairs while preserving early retention.

With maximum CRF already achieved, test a slightly shallower version of injection 9 for greater resolution margin at both critical pairs. Its 9.04-minute last peak leaves some room to improve separation without incurring a time penalty.

Preserve injection 13’s successful gradient slope exactly while trimming the unused high-organic portion. Its last peak eluted near phi = 0.57, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient with the same maximum CRF.

Test a gradient slope between injections 12 and 18, aiming to bring the R = 1.47 pair just above full resolution while shortening injection 12. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Test a modestly shallower version of injection 21 to increase separation of its R = 1.59 pair while checking whether the R = 1.52 pair remains resolved. This explores a maximum-score alternative with more balanced critical-pair margins and an expected last peak below 10 minutes.

Use a slope between injections 9 and 20 to balance their two critical-pair resolutions, targeting a minimum R near 1.7 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The trimmed endpoint should still place the last peak inside the gradient.

Trim injection 12’s unused gradient tail while preserving its exact slope and temperature, targeting the same maximum CRF and 8.00-minute last peak. The final organic fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.
